title: 3 O(n) operations consecutively nested, but still a total Big O of O(n^2). Why?
q_body: Question : "evaluate the average and the worst-case complexity, using the following notation : n = len(a)." def anagramme_list(a, b): # Time complexity : O(n^2) O(n^2) # Space complexity : ~O(n) (list made out of a string) res = False # O(1) O(1) if len(a) == len(b): # (cond O(1)) O(n^2) O(n^2) liste_b = list(b) # O(n) O(n) res = True # O(1) O(1) for i in a: # (it: O(n)) O(n^2) O(n^2) if i in liste_b: # (cond O(n)) O(n) O(n) liste_b.remove(i) # O(n) O(n) else: # O(1) O(1) res = False # O(1) O(1) return res I would've said that, in the worst case scenario, we got O(n^3) since there's an operation in O(n) (liste_b.remove(i)) triggered by a condition in O(n) (if i in liste_b) which is itself nested in a loop in O(n). No need to say that this answer surprised me... Could anyone please explain why is the nested operation in O(n) not considered to be "nested" in its parent (the 'if i in liste_b'), and, on a broader level, how to approach the big O evaluation in this type of case please ?

title: Grayskull slow in GitLab CI with local sdist
q_body: I’m generating a conda recipe from a local source distribution (sdist) using Grayskull . On my laptop (inside company intranet) it completes in ~30 seconds. In our GitLab CI pipeline (also inside the company intranet), the exact same command routinely takes ~20 minutes. Command: grayskull pypi ./my_package.tar.gz --output ./myoutput_dir Expectation: Because I’m pointing Grayskull at a local .tar.gz , I expected it to avoid contacting external services (PyPI/conda-forge/GitHub/etc.) and just emit a meta.yaml using the metadata bundled in the sdist. In CI I do not need dependency discovery against channels or any enrichment that requires the network; I only need a recipe skeleton generated from the local archive. Observed behavior: Local dev machine (intranet): ~30 seconds. GitLab CI job (intranet): ~20 minutes. Questions: Does Grayskull perform outbound network calls even when the input is a local sdist? Is there a flag or environment variable to force an offline/no-network run (skip any lookups against PyPI/conda-forge/ etc) so that recipe generation uses only what’s in the sdist?

title: How is the thread to be executed selected by the OS?
q_body: Why this question is different from Python Lock always re-acquired by the same thread . It may look similar because both questions use 2 threads. That question specifically requires each thread to execute once before handing over, creating an alternating foo,bar,foo,bar print pattern. It is looking for specific implementations to achieve that goal. This question is more open. It is not looking for a specific pattern, but an explanation of what I see, and direction on what variables matter (to tweak) to study this phenomena. import threading import time lock = threading.Lock() def high_priority(): while True: with lock: print("High priority thread acquired lock") time.sleep(0.2) def low_priority(): while True: with lock: print("Low priority thread acquired lock") # May never happen! time.sleep(0.1) t1 = threading.Thread(target=high_priority, daemon=True) t2 = threading.Thread(target=low_priority, daemon=True) t1.start() t2.start() time.sleep(1) I ran the code above 23 times before seeing low_priority get the lock. My aim is to understand what determines when within the 1 second sleep of main script low_priority thread gets the lock how often low_priority thread gets the lock However the experiments seem to require a long time so i'm looking for some theory first. Last 3 runs' output out of 23: ➜ deadlock python deadlock_priority.py High priority thread acquired lock High priority thread acquired lock High priority thread acquired lock High priority thread acquired lock High priority thread acquired lock ➜ deadlock python deadlock_priority.py High priority thread acquired loc
